solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Adverse reactions as in-law darns gross pants

indicators.note: in British slang pants means rubbish, so the letters before it are judged bad and reshaped

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a relative's clumsy sewing on their trousers is revolting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like the trousers being darned but is British slang for awful, the anagram signal acting on IN-LAW, DARNS and GROSS.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's phrase for the blows of outrageous fortune has become an idiom for hostile treatment or misfortune suffered.

clue.text: Head of science faculty gave away building down under

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, here taken from science

parts.note: hearing is one of the faculties, the senses
to shed is to give away or cast off

explanation.surface: A science faculty's dean donates a building in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faculty' looks like a university department but means one of the senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Australian sheep stations have a dedicated barn where the flock is clipped; down under is Australia and New Zealand.

clue.text: Doing time like an old native

definitions.meaning: someone doing time is in the can, slang for being in prison, read here as two words
of the Peruvian empire's people of long ago

explanation.definitionFit: Split in two the word is slang for imprisoned; whole, it describes the Andean empire's ancient people.

clue.text: Grand meeting with staff gathering in historical plant

parts.note: G is the usual abbreviation for grand, a thousand pounds
olden means of former times
a rod is a staff or stick

explanation.surface: A grand gathering of staff takes place in a historic plant or factory.
explanation.definitionFit: Solidago, a tall perennial with yellow flower spikes, is an example of a garden or wild plant.

clue.text: Nobbles about rising expenses

indicators.note: in a down clue a rising piece is read upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: CA, for circa, means about
costs are expenses

explanation.surface: Someone nobbles officials over rising expenses.
explanation.walkthrough: To nobble someone, in British slang, can be to buttonhole them.
explanation.definitionFit: To nobble can mean to waylay or buttonhole a person, which is to approach and address them boldly.

clue.text: Turn over cover on novel — Catch-22

indicators.note: turning the word over reverses its letters

parts.note: a lid is a cover
Emma is Jane Austen's novel

explanation.surface: Instructions to flip a book's cover to see Heller's novel Catch-22.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' points at Catch-22 the book, but Catch-22 is the definition and the novel is EMMA.
explanation.definitionFit: A Catch-22 is a no-win situation, a predicament with no good choice.

clue.text: Characters that could make mimic livid when 'bigged up'?

definitions.text: Characters that could make mimic livid when 'bigged up'?

parts.words: Characters that could make mimic livid when 'bigged up'?
parts.note: written in capitals, MIMIC and LIVID are made wholly of letters the ... used for counting: M, I, C, L, V and D

explanation.surface: Something that would infuriate an impressionist once exaggerated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bigged up' means written in upper case, not praised; the capitals of MIMIC and LIVID are all Roman number letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters such as I, V, X, L, C, D and M served as the ancient Romans' figures for counting.

clue.text: Smith's work is put here without due care

definitions.meaning: a blacksmith's horseshoe is nailed on to the foot of a horse
doing something hastily, while moving, without proper thought

explanation.definitionFit: A farrier's shoe goes on the horse's foot; the idiom also means acting improvised and without planning.

clue.text: Office software is better

explanation.definitionFit: Microsoft's spreadsheet program has a name that is also the verb meaning to outshine others.

clue.text: Ruth once associated with Jane?

definitions.meaning: ruth is an archaic word for sorrow or a cause of grief, a disaster
the frontierswoman Martha Jane Canary was known by this nickname before Jane

explanation.definitionFit: Archaic ruth meant grief or disaster, and the Wild West heroine was nicknamed this before Jane.

clue.text: Jack and Jill's bursary taken for this?

definitions.text: Jack and Jill's bursary taken for this?

parts.words: Jack and Jill's bursary taken for this?
parts.note: Jack and Jill went up the hill in a children's verse; bursary would be a rhyme for the first word of its type

explanation.surface: Two children have a grant to pay for something.
explanation.walkthrough: Read cryptically, Jack and Jill is the example and 'bursary' rhymes with nursery, so it could be taken as a rhyme for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack and Jill is a traditional children's verse, the sort sung to toddlers.

clue.text: From the start, referee irritates team …

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, taken here from referee

parts.note: angers means irritates

explanation.surface: A referee annoys a football side from kick-off.
explanation.walkthrough: Rangers is a Glasgow football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasgow's well-known Scottish football club is one example of a sports side.

clue.text: … another conceals drink in old cloak

indicators.note: one piece conceals another by holding it inside

parts.note: following the previous clue's team, another team is Man U, Manchester United
tea is a drink

explanation.surface: Continuing from the last clue, a second team hides drink inside an old cloak.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 'team' in the previous clue, so 'another' means another team: Man U is Manchester United.
explanation.definitionFit: A manteau was a loose cloak or gown worn in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

clue.text: Comparatively pleasant part of western precinct

indicators.note: in an across clue, going west means reading from right to left
a part of the word is a run of its letters

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood on the west side of a precinct is relatively agreeable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'western' seems to describe the precinct but tells you to read the hidden letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative form of an adjective meaning pleasant or agreeable.

clue.text: Clichés — teachers appearing in cases

indicators.note: one piece appears in another by being placed inside it

parts.note: chests are cases or boxes
NUT is the National Union of Teachers

explanation.surface: Clichés are exposed as teachers appear in court cases.
explanation.walkthrough: The NUT was Britain's National Union of Teachers.
explanation.definitionFit: An old chestnut is a joke or story repeated so often it has become stale, a cliché.

clue.text: Having interrupted drinks, drops off brief summaries

indicators.note: a piece interrupting another breaks into it and sits inside

parts.note: shots are small drinks of spirits
naps means drops off to sleep

explanation.surface: After disrupting a drinking session, someone falls asleep during short briefings.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick photograph is used figuratively for a short overview capturing a moment or situation.

clue.text: Engaged part of wheel, front almost spinning

parts.note: a spoke is part of a wheel

indicators.note: spinning letters are turned around into a new order
almost the whole word, missing its last letter

explanation.surface: A cyclist describes the front wheel's spoke turning while busy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims FRONT to FRON, then 'spinning' rearranges those letters to NFOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Something reserved or a person already betrothed is said to be claimed or taken, that is engaged.

clue.text: Over which, e.g., Picasso would proceed cautiously

definitions.text: Over which, e.g., Picasso would proceed cautiously

parts.words: Over which, e.g., Picasso would proceed cautiously
parts.note: Picasso was a painter; read the clue as a driver slowing over a ramp in the road

explanation.surface: The great Spanish painter approaches something carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as an artist's caution, but any driver, Picasso included, slows down over a road hump.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised ridge across a road forces motorists to slow and drive carefully over it.

clue.text: Opens cover of unknown mains left to be insulated

indicators.note: the cover of a word is its outside, the first and last letters of unknown
a piece insulated is wrapped inside another

parts.note: the main is the sea, so mains are seas

explanation.surface: An electrician opens the casing of unidentified mains wiring, leaving a wire to be insulated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mains' suggests electricity but is the poetic main, the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: To unseal a letter or container is to break its closure and open it.

clue.text: Fools put drink at bottom of trifle

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece at the bottom of another comes after it

parts.note: to trifle is to play or toy
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: Fools pour a drink at the base of a trifle dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: A trifle is a British layered dessert; here it is the verb meaning to toy.
explanation.definitionFit: To play up is to fool around or misbehave, as children do.

clue.text: Topless chest put forward

indicators.note: without its top, the word's first letter is removed

parts.note: a coffer is a chest for valuables

explanation.surface: A topless chest is pushed to the fore.
explanation.definitionFit: To present or propose something for consideration is to proffer it, put it forward.

clue.text: Attracts client services, always 50 per cent off

indicators.note: each word loses half its letters, here the front half, keeping the back half of client and services

explanation.surface: A firm lures customers with services permanently at half price.
explanation.walkthrough: '50 per cent off' reads as a sale but means halving each word, keeping the back halves ENT and ICES.
explanation.definitionFit: To lure or tempt someone is to attract them.

clue.text: Caught half-hearted grass with old conviction

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: with half its heart gone, one of the two middle letters is removed

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass

explanation.surface: Someone caught with weak cannabis has a previous conviction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grass' suggests cannabis and 'conviction' a court sentence; the latter means belief.
explanation.definitionFit: A creed or set of beliefs is a firmly held conviction.

clue.text: Peel, say, in England, banged up by state

indicators.note: banged up is slang for locked up, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: to aver is to state

explanation.surface: Robert Peel, the British politician, imprisoned by the state.
explanation.walkthrough: Peel suggests Sir Robert Peel, founder of the police, but is Emma Peel from the 1960s TV series The Avengers.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma Peel was one of the stylish agents in the British spy drama, an example of the type.

clue.text: Force something tedious to come up

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means reading upwards, reversing the letters

parts.note: a drag is something tedious

explanation.surface: Use force to make something boring surface.
explanation.walkthrough: The Garda is the Irish police force.
explanation.definitionFit: The national police service of Ireland is a force in the policing sense.

clue.text: See 6
Before close of play, keep score twice?

indicators.note: one piece comes before another in the answer

parts.note: a keep is the fortified tower of a castle, a fort

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter, here taken from play

explanation.surface: Before stumps, a cricketer keeps a double score.
explanation.walkthrough: A score is twenty, so twice a score is forty.
explanation.definitionFit: A score being twenty, doubling it gives the number that equals two such twenties.

clue.text: Rebecca possibly riding delightful horse in town

parts.note: Rebecca West was an English novelist
a rider is on a horse
super means delightful
a mare is a female horse

explanation.surface: Rebecca, perhaps, rides a lovely horse into town.
explanation.walkthrough: Weston-super-Mare is an English seaside town in Somerset.
explanation.definitionFit: The Somerset seaside resort on the Bristol Channel is a town.
